point-01.caption: Placement Before Ukeire
point-01.situation: A South-round hand that is not forced yet, where the order changes what every discard is worth. Two candidate tiles are close in shape, so points and future danger decide.
point-01.read: Ask what point change matters, then read the hand. A 1,000-point win that ends a dangerous dealer turn can be excellent from first and nearly useless from fourth. When LuckyJ leads and the tiles are close, it takes the safer one, but only when that tile still leaves the hand a way forward. If the order needs value, keep riichi, dora, and mangan material before the hand narrows. If the lead is the asset, make the next discard easier instead of chasing an upgrade you do not need.
point-01.whyNot: Keeping the most acceptance and deciding later feels clean. Later can be too late: by one-shanten the hand may already be locked into a result that does not matter, or into a live discard you never had to face.
point-01.copy: When two discards are close, say what you need: a cheap end, 5,200, mangan, or the lead protected. If the cheap line is enough, take the easier tile. If not, keep the tile that makes the hand worth pushing, as long as it is not dangerous right now.
point-01.limit: Do not use this to kill a clearly better shape. If one tile gives a strong tenpai or a much better wait and the safer tile only feels comfortable, take the real hand unless the scores make defense mandatory.

point-02.caption: Keep the Anchor
point-02.situation: An early, undecided hand: two-shanten or worse, several candidate blocks, and at least one pair, triplet, dora, red five, or yakuhai that could define it later. Nobody has forced a fold yet.
point-02.read: A good early anchor lets the hand become open, valuable, or defensible without a perfect run of draws. A pair or triplet can turn into a yakuhai call, toitoi pressure, a chiitoi fallback, or the pair of an ordinary hand. Dora and red-five shapes earn the same treatment when they make the final hand worth pushing. The tile has to have a concrete second job. Feeling important is not one.
point-02.whyNot: The pure-efficiency discard makes the hand look like a normal riichi hand right away. Many early hands are not normal yet, and forcing them to be can erase the best value or the open option before you know which draw is coming.
point-02.copy: In a messy early hand, mark the tiles that give yaku, dora value, a call, or an emergency stop. If one of them also helps the shape, keep it and cut the weak block that needs the most exact help.
point-02.limit: Do not protect anchors after their job expires. If the hand has a fast good-shape path, or the kept tile is a dead honor, an isolated terminal, or a pair that cannot become yaku, value, or safety, take the efficient discard.

point-03.caption: Open With a Reason
point-03.situation: A clumsy hand with a bad block or two, a possible yakuhai or tanyao, and an early call on offer. Taking it removes riichi, ura, and menzen tsumo. Nobody is forcing you to defend yet.
point-03.read: A call is strongest when it changes what the hand is allowed to do. A yakuhai pon makes the hand legal. A chi into tenpai changes the clock. A call that takes a draw from the dealer can be right even for a small hand. The usual open tanyao or yakuhai hand is worth 1,000 to 3,900, so the tempo has to be real to cover what you give up. LuckyJ calls often and passes often. Copy the selection, not the activity.
point-03.whyNot: Closed-hand thinking says pass, because riichi, ura, and tsumo are worth a lot. That is true when the hand can actually reach them. With two weak blocks, the closed 3,900 is often a story you tell yourself while an opponent wins a cheap hand first.
point-03.copy: Check yaku, distance, value, and the next safe tile. If the call gives a legal hand, immediate tenpai, a strong one-shanten, or a specific tempo gain, take it and discard the tile that keeps the hand coherent. Otherwise stay closed and let the table tell you more.
point-03.limit: This does not justify opening every bad shape. Good closed value, a live riichi path, a last-hand score that needs a bigger hand, or an open hand with no exit all argue for passing.

point-04.caption: Open, Keep Brakes
point-04.situation: You have called, or are about to, and the hand is not going to win right away. Honors, genbutsu, or suji tiles are competing with ordinary shape tiles for the last slots.
point-04.read: Open hands have fewer tiles to choose from, so they usually have to defend with what they kept before the threat appeared. A 1,000-point open hand still two-shanten should not casually spend its only genbutsu. A 3,900 tenpai can afford more. A saved genbutsu buys one turn, not a permanent fold. Once it is spent, the next draw decides whether mawashi still exists: a new genbutsu or a low-danger tile that keeps the one-shanten keeps the hand alive, a good tenpai can justify a fresh push, and if only a live tile keeps the shape the choice is a plain push or a fold. When you are fourth against a third-place dealer's riichi, winning also ends the dealer turn and stops the gap growing. Dealing straight into that dealer is the worst transfer, so wanting to stop them does not license a chain of unsafe discards.
point-04.whyNot: Efficiency says cut the safe honor and take the extra acceptance, because the hand is open and therefore attacking. It ignores the cost after the next call: choosing between folding with nothing and feeding a live tile for a cheap hand. The opposite mistake is treating fourth place as permission to push forever.
point-04.copy: Before calling, check distance and the remaining safe tile. After calling, check again: safe against whom, on which turn. Treat the last genbutsu as a one-turn option and start the count from zero once it is gone. Continue by mawashi while a low-danger tile keeps the shape, push when a draw makes a hand worth the danger, and break the hand when keeping it needs several live tiles. Being fourth against the third-place dealer adds value to winning, not to surviving one risky discard.
point-04.limit: Do not freeze the hand around a stale safe tile, and do not call every no-genbutsu continuation mawashi. Once no tolerable discard keeps the shape, mawashi has ended. If the hand is cheap, the wall is short, or more unsafe discards remain after this one, fold even from fourth.

point-05.caption: Trim Future Danger
point-05.situation: The hand is two-shanten or worse with a loose middle tile outside the value plan. Nobody has declared yet, but rivers are developing and some later releases are starting to look awkward.
point-05.read: A floater is not harmless because nobody has riichi yet. If the hand is slow, danger may arrive before your tenpai does, and an isolated [[4p]], [[5s]], or [[6m]] then has to be judged by what it costs to release later, not by what it accepts today. The idea is strongest when the tile is outside your yaku, outside your dora plan, and not part of the best five blocks. This is not an early fold. It removes the tile that would make a later push unreasonable.
point-05.whyNot: Efficiency keeps the central floater because it sees more tiles than a terminal or honor. In a fast hand that is right. In a slow hand it ignores the riichi the hand may have to survive first.
point-05.copy: When you are far away, name the value plan, then find the leftover tile least connected to it. If that tile is a live middle tile that will be hard to release later, cut it while the table is still cheap.
point-05.limit: Do not turn this into a reflex against middle tiles. Keep the floater when it is red, dora-connected, the only good-shape upgrade, or needed for the score you want.

point-06.caption: Seed Value Early
point-06.situation: An early hand whose fastest version looks cheap, but which still holds red fives, dora-adjacent tiles, a yakuhai pair, or a pair-heavy structure. The table is not forcing defense yet.
point-06.read: Value is easiest to keep while the hand is wide. If the efficient hand is 1,000 or 2,000 and the hanchan asks for 5,200 or mangan, the efficient line is already failing. LuckyJ's habit is narrow: keep red and dora material that still connects to tanyao, riichi, yakuhai, or a real pair structure. That is different from buying random risk from behind. A value tile earns its place by making the final hand worth pushing. When it stops improving the actual hand, it is clutter.
point-06.whyNot: The efficiency cut makes the hand cleaner right away and avoids holding an honor or dora too long. If that cleanliness produces a cheap, bad-shape tenpai you cannot push, the early speed bought nothing.
point-06.copy: When the cheap line is not enough, keep value material that is connected, pair-based, or callable, and spend terminals and spare floaters first. Recheck every draw. If the value tile starts costing real acceptance or real safety, let it go.
point-06.limit: This is not a license for broad risk because you are behind. Against live threats, or when the value tile is isolated and the hand stays small, choose shape or safety instead.

point-08.caption: Riichi Taxes Everyone
point-08.situation: A closed tenpai or near-tenpai where you can be the first to present a real threat. The choice is declare now, stay dama, or wait for a better upgrade.
point-08.read: Riichi turns pressure into points. It adds a han, creates ura upside, and makes every opponent price their next discard under threat. The question is not how often to reach. It is whether this declaration changes the table. Reach when the lock buys value, fold equity, or a placement swing you need. Stay quiet when it only buys a bad wait and a stick.
point-08.whyNot: The cautious mistake is waiting for the perfect wait after the hand is already strong enough. The reckless mistake is reaching every closed tenpai because riichi is usually good. Both ignore timing, opponent progress, and whether the value actually forces a reaction.
point-08.copy: If you are first to credible pressure, the wait is live, and the riichi turns a small hand into a real threat, declare. If the hand is already enough as dama, or the riichi only locks you into future danger, stay quiet. In review, check whether the riichi changed opponents' discards, not just whether it won.
point-08.limit: Avoid it against several active threats with a low-value bad wait, and in endgame score situations where dama wins the seat you need.

point-09.caption: Reprice Every Draw
point-09.situation: A playable hand where the table changes before you can win: a riichi appears, an open hand adds pressure, or your draw makes the next discard worse. The hand may need more than one unsafe discard to get home.
point-09.read: Push-fold is a sequence, not a single-tile question. The first discard may be fine on its own and the next draw can still turn the continuation into a bad contract. LuckyJ's most extreme pushes come from the nondealer Tokujou sample, 46 chosen discards at 90% or more on the maximum NAGA danger proxy, all against a riichi. The supported ones cluster in valuable tenpai, meaningful riichi declarations, and open hands with almost nothing left to fold with. The rejected ones show why the alarm still matters.
point-09.whyNot: Efficiency preserves acceptance and decides once that the hand is an attack. That misses the bill for the discards still to come and mistakes tenpai for permission. In the clearest rejected case, LuckyJ kept a late open tenpai while leading with 41,000 and dealt into a 12,000-point hand when a safe fold was available.
point-09.copy: Count value and distance, then count the unsafe discards the hand still owes. Before copying an extreme push, name what kind it is: value-backed tenpai, placement urgency, a pressure riichi, or a hand that called itself out of exits. If the hand is not tenpai or its value is ordinary, keep a safe exit or move through mawashi instead of paying the whole bill. When a new threat appears, count again from zero.
point-09.limit: These counts describe nondealer decisions only; do not mix dealer-continuation value into them. Outcomes were mixed, so a later win does not show the push was sound. A strong tenpai or a last-hand score need can still demand danger, but the value has to be explainable before the result is known.

point-10.caption: Count The Last Row
point-10.situation: The third row, with long rivers, at least one live threat, and a few draws left. You may be tenpai, one-shanten, or barely able to make keiten. Shape talk is no longer enough.
point-10.read: Late decisions are arithmetic. Count the direct win: value, wait, and whether it changes placement. Count draw tenpai: whether you can reach or keep it through genbutsu, suji, kabe, or other low-danger tiles. Count the fold: how many safe tiles you have and whether folding now protects placement better than a thin push. LuckyJ disagrees with NAGA far less in the late row than early, and that is a reminder that there is little room for style here.
point-10.whyNot: The tempting mistake is to keep using early-hand language: maybe value, maybe shape, maybe one more draw. In the third row, maybe is expensive. A tile that was flexible on turn five may now be a dangerous discard with no time left to cash its upside.
point-10.copy: With few draws left, write the decision in order: win value, tenpai-payment value, number of safe discards, and next-turn danger. If a discard advances one of those without creating a worse next discard, take it. Otherwise fold.
point-10.limit: Do not chase keiten through several live threats with an unprotected center tile. Do not overfold a high-value real tenpai just because the row is late, either.

point-11.caption: Keiten Is Value
point-11.situation: A late hand with few tiles left where an outright win is unlikely but tenpai is still reachable. The candidate discards differ mainly in safety and in whether they keep a final tenpai shape.
point-11.read: Noten payments are part of the hand's value. A 1,000 to 3,000 swing can protect first, pull you out of last, or force someone else to chase next hand. LuckyJ was tenpai at a little under half of its exhaustive draws, which is often enough to study rather than improvise. The right keiten chase uses genbutsu, dead tiles, kabe tiles, or tiles the threat has already accepted. The wrong chase asks a dangerous tile to pass because the wall is short.
point-11.whyNot: Pure defense is tempting because noten feels cheaper than a deal-in, and it often is. Pure attack is tempting because tenpai payments are visible and immediate. Both go wrong when they ignore the exact discard path.
point-11.copy: With the wall short, count how many safe or nearly safe discards get you to tenpai. If the answer is one or two harmless tiles, keep the shape and take the payment. If the answer includes a live middle tile against a real threat, fold and let the payment go.
point-11.limit: This does not apply when the hand still has a strong winning chance worth pushing normally. It also does not apply when tenpai needs more danger than the payment is worth.

point-12.caption: Splits Are Homework
point-12.situation: You are reviewing a hand where LuckyJ, Nishiki, the other NAGA heads, or Mortal disagree on the discard. The risk is treating one model's answer as a command instead of a question.
point-12.read: The method is conditional copying. LuckyJ matches NAGA's top discard about three times in four, so the mismatches are worth studying and a mismatch alone does not say who is right. The NAGA heads disagree among themselves, and Mortal often backs Nishiki or picks a third line. That forces you to separate blunders from style trade-offs and real insights. Copy the move only when you can state what it buys in points, safety, speed, pressure, or placement.
point-12.whyNot: It is easy to defer to the highest engine line because it feels objective, and just as easy to defer to LuckyJ because the book is about LuckyJ. Neither teaches you why a -3,900 risk is wrong in one hand and a +2,900 purchase is right in another.
point-12.copy: For every split, write three short claims before looking at the result: what LuckyJ bought, what the engine bought, and what each line risked. If LuckyJ's purchase is clear and repeatable, add it to your playbook. If you cannot explain it, file it as uncertain.
point-12.limit: Do not use engine disagreement to excuse fundamentals. Missed yaku, furiten, obvious betaori spots, and noten late pushes are still mistakes even when a model split makes them look clever.

point-13.caption: Price the Missing Yakuhai
point-13.situation: An opponent has opened without showing a yaku. You hold a loose dragon, the round wind, or their seat wind, and your own hand is not ready to punish them.
point-13.read: The live yakuhai may be the opponent's missing permission to win, so carrying it and discarding it both have a price. Discarding it offers the pon. It is not denial. The early line releases the tile while no yaku and no clear progress are visible, so it is not carried into a more dangerous turn. The later line holds it once calls, turn, or river make progress plausible.
point-13.whyNot: Holding the honor keeps the option of starving the open hand, and it can also become a dangerous live tile that blocks your own route. Releasing it keeps the shape and may hand the opponent a yaku. Price both instead of calling either one automatic defense.
point-13.copy: After every unclear call, mark dragons, the round wind, and that player's seat wind as possible yaku tiles. Release a singleton only while no yaku or clear progress is visible. Once progress is visible, hold it unless your own value, safety, or placement makes feeding acceptable.
point-13.limit: The selected examples are engine-contested. Treat the move as a stress test, not a default, and keep the tile when it is your pair, your yaku, your only safe tile, or part of a concrete value plan.

point-14.caption: Safety Has a Target
point-14.situation: You are choosing between trimming shape and keeping a tile that is genbutsu, suji, or otherwise safer against one opponent. There is a real or credible threat on the table, or one is likely soon.
point-14.read: Genbutsu is the strongest answer because it is a same-tile answer to one opponent's river. Suji is weaker but still practical when it points at the player you may have to fold against. The lesson is not to keep every safe-looking tile. It is to keep the one that turns a future forced live discard into a controlled fold. Most of these choices come before anyone declares, and a player's whole earlier river becomes safe against them the moment they riichi. In child rounds LuckyJ already held such a tile at 74.5% of 5,504 opponent declarations. Before a declaration the target is the most likely next attacker, and seat is the strongest signal: the dealer riichied in 21.0% of child kyoku against 17.7% for each child, and dealing into the dealer cost about 1.4 times as much. A strange river is a reason to start counting safe tiles, not a target by itself.
point-14.whyNot: Efficiency dislikes defensive clutter because the table may stay quiet. That is right when the tile has no opponent attached. It is wrong when spending the tile leaves your next bad draw with no answer to the dealer, the riichi player, or the open hand already applying pressure.
point-14.copy: Name the player first, then the event: riichi, second call, bad draw, or late keiten fight. If the tile is genbutsu or solid suji against that player and your hand is not strong enough to ignore danger, keep it over a marginal shape tile. Before anyone declares, name the most likely next attacker, usually the dealer, and keep a tile that already sits in that player's river. After a declaration, the declared player replaces the dealer as the name.
point-14.limit: Do not overrate generic safety. Weak suji, old outside tiles, and genbutsu against a quiet opponent should not block a good hand unless they also defend against the player likely to attack next. The dealer preference is a price rule, not a copied habit: on quiet tables LuckyJ discarded dealer-river tiles at 13.3% per turn against 12.4% for child-river tiles, so its own record shows no dealer bias.

point-15.caption: Stale Safety Costs Shape
point-15.situation: You hold a tile that was safe against someone earlier, but the table has moved on. Another player has riichi, an open hand is now the pressure, or your own hand is close enough that the old safe tile blocks tenpai.
point-15.read: Safe tiles expire. The previous chapter says keep safety for a specific opponent. This one says spend it when that opponent is no longer the problem. LuckyJ's stale-safety spends came with a current-danger check, and its threat-specific keeps held up just as well, so the rule cuts both ways: keep live safety, spend dead safety. Letting a real hand decay into a noten draw because you protected against the wrong player is not careful play.
point-15.whyNot: Keeping a safe-looking tile feels disciplined. Often it is only fear with a label. If the tile does not answer the live riichi or the player most likely to win, holding it damages your shape and can waste your next good draw.
point-15.copy: Identify the current danger, then compare your safe tiles against that player. If the old tile protects a quiet opponent, you have another real safe tile, and the hand is close enough to care about shape, discard the stale tile. Otherwise keep the brake.
point-15.limit: Do not spend stale-looking safety in thin late hands with no second safe tile, when the original opponent is still the main threat, or when betaori is already the best result.

point-16.caption: Attack Through Edges
point-16.situation: A middle or late hand close enough that keeping tenpai shape matters, with enough danger that a lower-friction discard has value. The choice is an outside tile against a middle tile that keeps the hand connected.
point-16.read: A terminal discard can be an attacking discard when it buys the right to keep the center. Middle tiles connect three-away shapes: [[3p]][[4p]] wants [[2p]] or [[5p]], [[6p]][[7p]] wants [[5p]] or [[8p]], and the tile between them often keeps both alive. If the outside tile does not support value, yaku, a pair, or real safety, it is weaker than it looks. That is why LuckyJ often spends the edge and keeps the inner line.
point-16.whyNot: Terminals feel safe and middle tiles feel dangerous, so the reflex is to cut the middle tile. If the middle tile is the bridge to a good tenpai, cutting it turns a real hand into a pile of safer leftovers.
point-16.copy: When an outside cut looks strange, look at the tile you keep. If the kept middle tile forms a ryanmen, repairs a bad block, keeps a perfect one-shanten, or avoids a worse live discard next turn, the edge cut is usually the practical attack.
point-16.limit: This does not apply when the outside tile has a stronger job than the center. Dora terminals, chiitoi pairs, honitsu or chanta material, and exact genbutsu against the main threat come first.

point-18.caption: Label the Honor
point-18.situation: Your hand holds one or more honors while the table is still changing. Some may be your own yakuhai, some may be useful to an open opponent, and some may be nothing but defensive material.
point-18.read: Give the honor a role first, because different roles produce opposite discards. Self-value honors stay when they create yaku, pair value, honitsu, chiitoi, or dora scaling. Honors that could be an opponent's yaku go early when an unclear open hand could use them. Dead honors and genbutsu honors are defensive material, but only against the threats they actually answer. Strong honor play is role-first, not yakuhai-first or yakuhai-last.
point-18.whyNot: The easy habit is one slogan: cut honors early, keep honors for safety, or hold yakuhai pairs forever. Each wins some hands and ruins others. Without the role label you cannot tell whether the tile is earning value for you, handing a yaku to someone else, or buying a future fold.
point-18.copy: For each honor, ask four questions in order: is it my yaku or value, is it someone else's missing yaku, is it dead, and is it safe against the real threat? Play the strongest answer. If two roles conflict, use score and distance: a slow hand from behind values self yaku more, a lead against riichi values defense more.
point-18.limit: Do not keep a label out of habit. Recheck after every call, riichi, second visible copy, and late abnormal river. One pon can change both legality and danger at once.
